paras: The killing of Leslie Allen was the shooting death of a 22-year-old Black hotel porter by a posse of Halifax County citizens near Virgilina, Virginia, on the morning of August 26, 1920. Allen had been accused of insulting two white girls at the Buffalo Hotel and of shooting James Baptist, a white man who tried to seize him. Some papers headlined the killing as a lynching, and one reported that the governor of Virginia would investigate.

According to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, Allen was from Alabama, had lately lived in Petersburg, where he drove for a man named Parham, and had worked as a porter at the Buffalo Hotel for two weeks. On the evening of August 25, two girls who set up tenpins on the hotel grounds said he demanded to bowl as they were closing the alley. When they said only white patrons had the privilege, he was said to have made "highly objectionable remarks" and "cursed the white race."

Baptist, described as a wealthy Halifax County resident, went with a few men to apprehend Allen at Buffalo station. By the Richmond account Allen fired eighteen shots from two revolvers at the unarmed party, while the United Press counted twenty; one bullet struck Baptist in the chest, and he was taken to a hospital in South Boston. A posse with bloodhounds searched the country around Buffalo Lithia through the night without finding him.

Early on August 26, R. E. Amos, a Virgilina merchant, grew suspicious of a stranger at his store who gave his name as "John Brown" and said he had worked at the Buffalo Hotel. After checking the description with the South Boston police by telephone, Amos alerted the posse and placed farmers to hem the man in. The trail led to the house of George Burrell, a Black tenant, two miles from Virgilina, which the Richmond paper placed in Mecklenburg County.

The Times-Dispatch reported that ten armed men found a figure under bedding upstairs, that a shot from it struck Mason Elam in the foot, and that the men then "poured several volleys into the writhing bed quilts." The Associated Press instead said that Marse Elam, Baptist's brother-in-law, crawled up to the crouching man and killed him with a shotgun. Both versions agree that Allen's head was nearly torn away, and the body was taken to Buffalo and turned over to the sheriff.

The posse said it had held a warrant for Allen's arrest and that there was "no doubt" he had fired at Elam. A Norfolk dispatch in the Washington Times on August 28 said Governor Davis would investigate, but no further report of an investigation, inquest or arrest was found.

The Associated Press story that ran on August 26 in Topeka, Chattanooga, Ocala, Cordele and Lakeland described an "unidentified negro" and led with the charge of insulting white girls, as in the Cordele headline "Negro Shot to Death for Insulting Two White Girls." The next day the Birmingham Age-Herald headed the same wire "Virginians Lynch an Unknown Negro," and the Montgomery Advertiser, noting that Allen was from Alabama, headed its version "Alabama Negro Is Summarily Lynched." The United Press version, carried in Washington and Alexandria, attributed its account to "word brought back from a posse."

The Richmond Times-Dispatch gave the fullest account on its front page under the headline "Posse Kills Negro Who Shot Down Halifax Man," with the subhead "Pays With Life for Wounding James Baptist." Its narrative relied on the posse and repeated its assurance that it had "made no mistake." A short item naming Allen ran in South Bend and Omaha, and a one-sentence version circulated in a syndicated news column in Western weeklies in early September.
The only Black-press notice found was that syndicated sentence, printed without comment among general news in the Colorado Statesman of September 4.

The Washington Times dispatch differed from every other report, placing the killing in a thicket near Norfolk on Wednesday night by a posse of 300 and naming the wounded man "John Baptiste." Reports also differed on whether Elam fired the fatal shot or was himself wounded before ten men fired, and on whether one or two pursuers were hit.

reader.title: Killing of Leslie Allen
bases: A posse of Halifax County citizens with bloodhounds tracked a Black man accused of insulting two white girls and shooting a white man, and killed him in a house near Virgilina (A8, A9, A6).

A posse of armed citizens, ten of whom fired volleys into the bedding where he lay, killed Allen on accusations of insulting white girls and shooting Baptist (A9, A8); the posse said it held a warrant and had been fired on (A9), but several papers headlined the killing a lynching and one reported a governor's investigation (A10, A11, A16).
Independent Associated Press, United Press and Richmond Times-Dispatch reports agree that a posse with bloodhounds killed the man near Virgilina on Aug. 26 after he shot James Baptist (A1, A12, A8).

accounts.label: Associated Press (early)
accounts.gist: An unidentified man charged with insulting two white girls was tracked by a posse with bloodhounds and killed at Virgilina by Marse Elam after wounding a pursuer.

accounts.label: Richmond Times-Dispatch (Danville correspondent, posse's account)
accounts.gist: Allen fired 18 shots at Baptist's unarmed party, was traced through Amos to Burrell's house, shot Elam from under the bedding, and was killed when ten men poured volleys into the quilts; the posse said it had a warrant.

accounts.label: United Press
accounts.gist: The man who shot Baptist after a dispute over tenpins was cornered and shot to death 'in a camp', according to word brought back by the posse.

accounts.label: Washington Times (Norfolk dispatch)
accounts.gist: An unidentified man was killed in a thicket near Norfolk on Wednesday night by a posse of 300; Governor Davis would investigate.

accounts.label: Syndicated news column
accounts.gist: One sentence: Leslie Allen was shot and killed near Virgilina by a posse of Halifax County citizens after charges he insulted two small white girls.

framing.detail: Richmond Times-Dispatch headlined 'Posse Kills Negro Who Shot Down Halifax Man' and 'Pays With Life for Wounding James Baptist', and repeated the posse's assurance that 'there is no doubt' of his guilt.
AP reprints headlined the insult charge: 'Insulted White Girls—Shot', 'Negro Shot to Death for Insulting Two White Girls', 'Virginia Negro Who Insulted Girl Shot by Citizens'.
Birmingham and Montgomery headed the same wire 'Virginians Lynch an Unknown Negro' and 'Alabama Negro Is Summarily Lynched'.
Washington Times headlined 'Virginia Governor to Probe Negro Lynching'.
Colorado Statesman ran the one-sentence syndicated item among general news, without headline or comment.
